name: sound-cues
title: Sound cues
description: Sounds for events with a mute, driven by a manifest of sound files, for web, Apple and Android.

facilities.description: Sound cues for events, a manifest of sounds, mute by the device's sound preference

text.purpose: `sound-cues` plays short sounds for what happens in an application. A manifest lists the sound files (cues) and which cues each event plays, in order and with delays, so an event such as "cards revealed" can play a deal sound then, 300 ms later, a flip sound. The application sends events by name and never touches audio; the files and the event names stay with the application (the recipe ships its own manifest and files). Sound is on or off by the device's `sound` preference from the `preferences` component, turning it off stops everything playing or waiting; a host can also forbid sound for now (a shared display). Browsers allow sound only after a tap, so nothing plays until the first one unlocks it. The component knows nothing about poker or any other game.
text.userInputs: `soundManifest`: the folder name that holds `manifest.json` and the sound files (lower-case letters, digits and hyphens; an aepm string setting cannot hold a slash or a dot, so it is a name not a path), default `sounds`. `defaultMuted`: whether sound starts muted when the device has no recorded preference, default false; give the preferences component `soundPreferenceDefault(defaultMuted)` as its default for `sound` so both agree. The manifest is `{ "format": 1, "cues": { "tap": "tap.wav" }, "events": { "button": ["tap"], "reveal": [{ "cue": "deal" }, { "cue": "flip", "delayMs": 300 }] } }`; files end in wav, mp3, ogg, m4a, aac or caf and are relative paths with no `..`.
text.integration: Web: `createCues({ manifest, baseUrl: "./sounds", preferences, allowed })`, then `cues.unlockOn(document)` so the first tap unlocks sound, and `cues.emit("event")` wherever something happens; wire a sound toggle to `cues.setMuted`. `preferences` is the preferences component's store (only `get`, `set` and `subscribe` of `sound` are used); without it mute is kept in memory. Apple: parse the manifest with `SoundCueModel.parseManifest`, make a `SoundCuePlayer(manifest:locate:isMuted:allowed:)` where `locate` finds files in the bundle and `isMuted` reads `SoundCueModel.isMuted(sound:defaultMuted:)`; call `stopAll()` when sound is turned off. Android: `ManifestJson.parse` the manifest, package the files as raw resources named by `CueModel.rawResourceName` (tap.wav becomes `snd_tap`), make a `SoundCuePlayer(manifest, isMuted, allowed)` and call `init(context)`, `emit(event)`, and `stopAll()` when sound is turned off. Which events exist, the sounds themselves, call audio and the other players' voices stay with the recipe.
text.infrastructure: None. Local audio only; no accounts, network (beyond fetching the application's own sound files on the web) or deployment.
text.verification: Node tests check manifest validation (every kind of fault), event plans, settings, file and resource names and the mute rule, and run the engine against a fake audio context: nothing plays before unlock, a cue loads once and may overlap, events play their cues at the planned delays, muting stops playing and still-loading sounds and unmuting plays again, `defaultMuted` and a stored preference decide the state (a stored value wins), turning sound off in the preferences stops it, a host can forbid sound, and a missing file is silent; and that the OpenRPC interface's name and file patterns agree with the validator, its settings match the defaults, and every method it lists is an exported web function or player operation. The Apple check compiles and runs `tests/apple/main.swift` for macOS, comparing plans, resource names and the mute rule with the TypeScript output, refusing faulty manifests and exercising the player with no files, then type-checks the Swift for the iOS simulator. The Android check compares the same plans (`tests/android/Expected.kt`); kotlinc was not available where this was written, so it has not been run, and `SoundCuePlayer.kt` and `ManifestJson.kt` need the Android SDK and are compiled by the application's Gradle build. No audio output is heard by any check.
text.scenarios: A button press emits `button` and a click plays; revealing cards emits `reveal` and a deal sound is followed 300 ms later by a flip; the player taps the sound toggle, everything stops and later events stay silent; on a shared display the host forbids sound; a recipe with its own sounds and event names supplies its own manifest folder.
text.updates: Patch updates replace files only. The component keeps no data of its own (the sound preference is kept by the preferences component); removal deletes its files and the application's imports of them.

agentInstructions: Select `ourapps-ae/sound-cues`; connect `preferences` to the preferences component's output. Set `soundManifest` to the folder the recipe's sound files and manifest live in, and `defaultMuted` only if the user wants sound off to begin with. The event names in the manifest come from the recipe; do not invent them here.
developerInstructions: Supply the sound files and a `manifest.json` in the folder named by `soundManifest`; keep them short and quiet if microphones may be open. On the web serve the folder next to the page and pass its URL as `baseUrl`; on Apple add the files to the bundle; on Android add them as raw resources named as `rawResourceName` says. Call `unlock` (or `unlockOn`) from a user tap on the web.

suitability.notes: Pure library; no provider limits apply.
